questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Your school has set aside a week in which every student must learn a new skill, and you have decided to join the swimming group even though deep water frightens you. Write an e-mail of about 100 words to your friend, telling what you have decided to do, why you are facing this fear now, and asking your friend to join you.

markingPoints.description: Uses the e-mail format: a subject line, a greeting, the body and a closing signature.
States the skill chosen and the fact that deep water frightens the writer.
Explains why the writer is facing the fear now, choosing the skill that frightens him most rather than going on avoiding it.
Makes the request, asking the friend to come to the pool, and gives a reason for it.
Keeps to about 100 words in a friendly, informal register with correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Subject: Learning to Swim
Dear friend,
I have decided to join the swimming group this week. Deep water has always frightened me, and for years I made excuses to stay out of it. Now I have chosen the very skill that frightens me most, because I would rather try and fail than go on avoiding it. I know it will take courage to let go and trust the water to hold me up. Please come with me to the pool and stand beside me while I learn. I will feel braver with you there.
Yours,
A Class 10 student

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write an article of about 100 words for your school magazine, with the heading My First Attempt, on the challenges of learning your first new skill and on how you overcame your fear of it.

markingPoints.description: Uses the article format: a suitable heading and a clear beginning, middle and end.
Describes the fear at the start and the moment of running back, showing the writer’s hesitation.
Explains how the fear was overcome, such as a family member running beside the writer and holding the seat.
Ends with the writer riding to school alone, showing the change.
Keeps to about 100 words in a lively, descriptive style with correct grammar, spelling and punctuation.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
My First Attempt
Nobody in my family rides a bicycle, so when my father wheeled an old one out for me I was frightened of it. I stood over it for a long time, one foot on the pedal, waiting for the machine to topple me. Then my father ran beside me, holding the seat, and told me to keep pedalling. The moment he let go, my hands shook and I ran back. The next day I asked for the bicycle again, and again I ran back. At last he stopped running, and I rode to school on my own.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Your school is holding an assembly on the theme Face Your First Fear. Write a speech of about 100 words for the Principal to deliver at that assembly, saying why young people should attempt the thing they are most afraid of.

markingPoints.description: Opens with a suitable greeting to the assembly and states the theme of the speech.
Gives at least two examples of things young people are afraid of, such as speaking in front of a crowd, diving into a pool, or asking a question in class.
Explains the cost of avoidance, that the fear grows larger each time it is avoided.
Uses the image of a young bird that would not leave its ledge, and what changed matters: patience and a reward rather than scolding.
Ends with an appeal to the audience and keeps to about 100 words in a formal register with correct grammar and spelling.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Good morning, teachers and dear friends,
Every one of us has one task we keep putting off. It may be speaking in front of a crowd, diving into a pool, or asking a question in class. We call these things small, but they grow larger every time we avoid them, until the fear itself keeps us from trying. I remember a young bird that would not leave its ledge while the rest of its family flew out over the sea. What changed matters was not a lecture but patience, and food held out until hunger was stronger than doubt. So choose the one thing you fear most and go at it while the year is young. Thank you.

Paris was about 150 kilometres behind me when

They looked like black mountains standing in front

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Explain, in about 120 words and in clear steps, how the young seagull overcomes his fear of flying, from the moment he dived at the fish to the moment he was floating on the green sea.

markingPoints.description: He dived at the fish and fell outwards and downwards into space, seized by a monstrous terror.
The terror lasted only a minute, and then he felt his wings spread outwards with the wind against them.
He was no longer falling headlong but soaring gradually downwards and outwards, and he was no longer afraid.
One flap of his wings lifted him upwards and he joined the circling flight of his family.
He dropped his legs to stand on the green sea; his feet and then his belly sank in and he floated.
His family screamed and praised him and offered him scraps of dog-fish, and he had made his first flight.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish and fell outwards and downwards into space.
2. A monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still; he could hear nothing, but it lasted only a minute.
3. Then he felt his wings spread outwards and the wind rush against his breast feathers and under his stomach.
4. He was not falling headlong now; he was soaring gradually downwards and outwards, and he was no longer afraid.
5. He flapped his wings once and soared upwards, while his mother, his father, his brothers and his sister flew around him.
6. At last he dropped his legs to stand on the green sea; his feet and belly sank in and he floated while his family screamed and praised him.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Explain, in about 120 words and in clear steps, how the narrator’s journey to safety is made possible even though his compass, his radio and his fuel have all failed.

markingPoints.description: His compass spun uselessly, the other instruments went dead and Paris Control did not answer, leaving him lost.
There was only enough fuel in his last tank to fly for five or ten minutes more.
He saw another aeroplane near him in the black clouds, with no lights on its wings, and the pilot waved and told him to follow.
The pilot turned slowly to the north and then began to go down, and the narrator followed him through the storm.
He came out of the clouds and saw two long straight lines of lights, a runway and an airport, so he was safe.
The black aeroplane was gone, and the woman at the control centre said that no other aeroplanes were flying that night.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Inside the storm the compass spun uselessly, the other instruments went dead and Paris Control did not answer, so he was lost.
2. There was only enough fuel in his last tank to fly for five or ten minutes more.
3. Then he saw another aeroplane quite near him in the black clouds, with no lights on its wings.
4. The pilot lifted one hand and waved and told him to follow, turning slowly to the north so he could be seen.
5. The pilot began to go down and the narrator followed him out of the clouds.
6. He saw two long straight lines of lights, a runway and an airport, so he was safe; but the black aeroplane was gone.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Compare the young seagull’s situation on his ledge with the pilot’s situation in the storm clouds, and explain in about 120 words, in clear steps, how each of them is finally set free.

markingPoints.description: The young seagull is held on his ledge by fear: the sea below is a long way down and he is sure his wings will never support him.
His parents threaten to let him starve, and when scolding fails his mother flies across with a piece of fish and halts just beyond his beak.
Maddened by hunger he dives for the fish and floats at last on the green sea, so his first flight sets him free.
The pilot is trapped in the storm clouds because his compass and radio fail and his fuel is finished.
A black aeroplane with no lights on its wings comes near him, its pilot waves and tells him to follow, staying in front so that he can be seen.
With five or ten minutes of fuel left, the stranger goes down, the narrator follows out of the clouds and lands beside a runway.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. The young seagull is held on his ledge by fear: the sea below is a long way down and he is sure his wings will never support him.
2. His parents threaten to let him starve; when scolding fails, his mother flies across with a fish and halts just beyond his beak.
3. Maddened by hunger he dives for the fish and floats at last on the green sea, so his first flight sets him free.
4. The pilot is trapped in storm clouds: his compass and radio fail and his fuel is finished.
5. A black aeroplane with no lights on its wings comes near him; its pilot waves and says ‘Follow me’, staying in front.
6. With five or ten minutes of fuel left, the stranger goes down and the narrator follows out of the clouds to a runway.
